articles.subject: science
articles.title: Earth: The Blue Planet
articles.summary: Why our world looks so watery from space.
articles.content:
From space, Earth looks mostly **blue** because oceans cover so much of the surface. Oceans store heat, make weather, and are home to countless animals.

Even if you live far from the coast, rain that falls on meadows may have evaporated from the sea long ago. The ocean and the land are connected through the **water cycle**.

articles.subject: geography
articles.title: Oceans and the Water Cycle
articles.summary: How seas feed clouds and rain.
articles.content:
The Sun warms the ocean surface. Water **evaporates**, rises, forms clouds, and later falls as **precipitation**. Rivers return much of that water to the sea.

Oceans are the giant engine of Earth’s water cycle. When ocean temperatures change, weather patterns far inland can change too.

articles.subject: science
articles.title: Why Is the Ocean Salty?
articles.summary: Dissolved minerals from land and vents.
articles.content:
Rain washes tiny amounts of minerals from rocks into rivers. Rivers carry those minerals to the sea. Over long ages, salts build up in the ocean.

That is why ocean water tastes salty and is not for drinking without special treatment. Different seas can be a bit more or less salty depending on rivers, ice, and evaporation.

articles.subject: science
articles.title: Tides: The Ocean’s Daily Rise and Fall
articles.summary: How the Moon helps pull the sea.
articles.content:
**Tides** are regular rises and falls of sea level along coasts. The **Moon’s gravity** pulls on Earth’s oceans (the Sun helps too).

As Earth turns, shorelines move through tidal bulges, so many places see high and low tide each day. Tide pools left at low tide are great places to spot small ocean creatures — carefully and without harming them.

articles.subject: science
articles.title: How Waves Form
articles.summary: Wind energy dancing across the surface.
articles.content:
Most waves you see at a beach start with **wind**. Air friction transfers energy into the water surface. Stronger, longer winds over more distance make bigger waves.

Waves move energy; water particles mostly bob in place until the wave breaks near shore. Surfers ride that moving energy — carefully, with respect for the ocean’s power.

articles.subject: geography
articles.title: Ocean Currents: Highways of Water
articles.summary: Moving heat and life around the planet.
articles.content:
**Currents** are large-scale flows of ocean water. Winds, Earth’s rotation, temperature, and salinity all help shape them.

Currents carry warm and cold water, nutrients, and plankton. They influence climates of coastal cities and the routes ships choose. Scientists track currents with satellites, floats, and models to understand weather and climate.

articles.subject: science
articles.title: Homes in the Sea
articles.summary: Reefs, kelp forests, and open water.
articles.content:
The ocean is not one single habitat. It includes:
- **Coral reefs** — busy cities of fish and coral
- **Kelp forests** — tall seaweed “trees”
- **Open ocean** — wide blue water
- **Deep sea** — dark, cold, and mysterious

Each place has animals adapted to its light, temperature, and food. Protecting habitats helps protect the animals that need them.

articles.subject: science
articles.title: Coral Reefs: Living Walls
articles.summary: Tiny animals that build big ecosystems.
articles.content:
**Corals** are animals. Many reef-building corals host tiny algae that share food from sunlight. Together they build rocky structures over long times.

Reefs shelter huge numbers of species. When water gets too warm or polluted, corals can **bleach** and weaken. Scientists and communities work to reduce stress and protect remaining reefs.

articles.subject: science
articles.title: Who Eats Whom in the Ocean?
articles.content:
Most ocean food webs start with tiny **phytoplankton** that make food from sunlight. Zooplankton eat them; small fish eat plankton; larger fish, seals, and sharks eat smaller animals.

If one link is damaged by overfishing or pollution, effects can ripple through the web. That is why ocean health matters even if you never go fishing yourself.

image.alt: Who Eats Whom in the Ocean?

articles.subject: science
articles.title: Ocean Mammals
articles.summary: Whales, dolphins, and seals — air breathers at sea.
articles.content:
Not every ocean animal is a fish! **Whales**, **dolphins**, and **seals** are **mammals**. They breathe air with lungs, are warm-blooded, and feed milk to babies.

Whales may dive deep, but they must return to the surface to breathe. Watching them (from a safe distance) is a reminder that the ocean is full of surprising lives.

articles.subject: science
articles.title: The Deep Sea
articles.content:
Below the sunlit surface, light fades quickly. The **deep sea** is cold, dark, and under crushing pressure. Yet life thrives near **hydrothermal vents**, on abyssal plains, and in midwater with **bioluminescent** animals.

Humans explore with **submersibles** and **ROVs** because divers cannot safely go that deep unaided. Every expedition still finds species new to science.

articles.subject: science
articles.title: Oceans and Climate
articles.summary: Heat storage, carbon, and changing seas.
articles.content:
Oceans absorb huge amounts of heat and carbon dioxide. That slows some atmospheric warming but also causes **ocean warming**, **sea-level rise** (from expansion and melting ice), and **acidification** that stresses shell-builders.

Understanding ocean climate helps societies prepare for storms, fisheries shifts, and coastal change. Science tools include satellites, tide gauges, and drifting Argo floats.

articles.subject: technology
articles.title: Exploring the Ocean
articles.content:
We map and study oceans with many tools:
- **Research ships** collect samples
- **Sonar** measures depth with sound
- **Satellites** watch temperature and color from space
- **ROVs and AUVs** explore where people cannot easily go

Ocean exploration is still young compared with maps of land — most of the deep seafloor remains only roughly charted.

articles.subject: science
articles.title: Protecting the Ocean
articles.summary: What kids and communities can understand and support.
articles.content:
Healthy oceans need less pollution, smarter fishing, and protected habitats. Helpful ideas include:
- Reducing single-use plastics and never littering
- Supporting **marine protected areas**
- Choosing sustainable seafood when adults shop
- Learning and sharing accurate science

Small actions add up when millions of people join in. The ocean is vast — and worth caring for.

articles.subject: history
articles.title: Ocean Science History Highlights
articles.summary: From ancient voyaging to modern oceanography.
articles.content:
People have read coasts and currents for millennia. **Polynesian wayfinders** crossed the Pacific using stars and swells. Later, scientific voyages such as the **Challenger expedition** (1870s) helped found modern **oceanography** by measuring depths, chemistry, and life worldwide.

Today’s global observing systems continue that mission with robots and satellites — a partnership of exploration and data.

articles.subject: geography
articles.title: Coasts and Beaches
articles.summary: Where land and sea shake hands.
articles.content:
A **coast** is where land meets the ocean. **Beaches** form from sand, pebbles, or shells moved by waves. Storms can reshape a beach in a single night!

Coasts are fun places to visit. Stay safe: watch waves, listen to lifeguards, and leave living creatures where they belong.

articles.subject: science
articles.title: Fishy Facts
articles.content:
Most fish use **gills** to take oxygen from water. **Fins** help them steer and swim. Many have **scales** that protect their bodies.

Fish live in shallow reefs, open ocean, cold polar seas, and deep dark waters. Some school together for safety; others hide in sand or coral.

articles.subject: technology
articles.title: Ocean Careers
articles.summary: Jobs that study and protect the sea.
articles.content:
People who work with oceans include:
- **Marine biologists** — study living things
- **Oceanographers** — study water, climate, and seafloor
- **Engineers** — build ships, sensors, and robots
- **Conservationists** — protect habitats and species
- **Educators** — teach others what the ocean needs

Curiosity, careful measurement, and teamwork matter more than any single superpower.
